HEADLINE: The GST success shows up the carbon tax failure
TEXT:
On the eve of the 20th anniversary of the goods and services tax, Scott Morrison has thankfully not ruled out including an increase in the GST rate, or broadening its base, as part of a tax reform package to make the economy more efficient and, yes, create jobs. This is important coming ahead of the Thodey review of federal-state financial relations commissioned by NSW Treasurer Dominic Perrottet. As former foreign minister Alexander Downer wrote on these pages yesterday, a tax package that included higher and broadened GST would not only allow for cuts to personal income and company tax but also reform of inefficient and distorting state taxes including "payroll tax - that tax on jobs".

The idea of shifting the burden of taxation from income to consumption is well rehearsed in Australia. By the time John Howard and Peter Costello introduced the tax in 2000, it had been preceded by a quarter-century of debate, pursued by both sides of politics. That helped Mr Howard to win a mandate for a 10 per cent GST at the 1998 election, despite having recanted his 1996 election promise "never ever" to do so.

Yet the simple idea of putting more of the tax burden on spending rather than on productive work, investment and saving was complex to translate into practice. Paul Keating used this complexity to resort to scaremongering about John Hewson's proposed 15 per cent GST - including on birthday cakes! - even in the shadow of the previous recession. Consequently, the ability to politically sell the GST within a decade of the Coalition losing the "unloseable" 1993 election required mastery of detail from Mr Howard and Mr Costello.

Contrast this challenge with the debacle of the Rudd government's Resource Super Profits Tax, plucked and repackaged from the 2010 Henry tax review, which was banned from considering lifting the rate or broadening the base of the GST. Ken Henry's review set out a solid intellectual justification for taxing the "rents" - or above-"normal" profits - derived from Australia's non-renewable natural resources. But the details of the "Brown tax" or "net cash flow tax" were difficult to understand and launched with no tilling of the political ground. Its packaging as a "super profits" tax revealed its purpose as a politicised revenue grab to finance Labor's spending monuments by plundering the industry most responsible for modern Australia's prosperity.

The whole notion of taxing mining "rents" - which implied unearned or undeserved "excessive" profits - struck at the success of the nation's internationally competitive mining industry, which took the risk of putting hundreds of billions of dollars into generating profits, taxes and jobs from otherwise worthless buried rocks. Miners capitalise on Australia's competitive advantage in natural mineral deposits by having the expertise to develop efficient, high-tech production and global supply

chains. The elevated risks of such highly cyclical and

capital-intensive pursuits, exposed to all manner of technical, physical, political and geopolitical risks over decades-long time frames, require commensurate returns. Taxing away the supposed excess or super profits risked turning away the capital in first place.

The debacle of Labor's mining tax was followed shortly afterwards by the fiasco of Labor's carbon tax. Kevin Rudd abandoned a carbon price at Julia Gillard's urging when the politics became difficult. After toppling Mr Rudd, Ms Gillard promised before the 2010 election that there would be no carbon tax under a government she led - only to subsequently bring in a fixed carbon price in cahoots with the Greens.

The irony is that a revenue-neutral carbon price or tax that helped fund a reduction in enterprise-dulling income tax would be the least costly way of reducing carbon emissions. Yet the ground has been so poisoned that neither side of politics wants to go anywhere near conceding this.

The ground has been so poisoned by the Rudd and Gillard debacles that neither side of politics wants to go anywhere near a price on carbon.

HEADLINE: Barrister calls out Gleeson on court secrecy
TEXT:
A Victorian barrister and former High Court of Australia associate says former chief justice Murray Gleeson, pictured, needs to break "the culture of secrecy" and comment about what, if anything, he knows of the alleged behaviour of Dyson Heydon, some of which occurred under his watch.

Kathleen Foley, a High Court associate in 2004 and 2005 to Kenneth Hayne, says it is not good enough that Mr Gleeson has declined to comment so far on findings that Mr Heydon harassed his associate Rachael Patterson Collins and five others.

"It is time for the culture of silence to be broken," Ms Foley writes in today's The Australian Financial Review.

"But that kind of change cannot be borne only by those brave women who have come forward.

"The leaders of the profession must step up. Those who have enjoyed their time at the very top - and who continue to enjoy the spoils of our profession - need to rethink the habits of a lifetime and ask whose interests are being served by continuing to adhere to a culture which is so plainly in need of fixing.

"There can be no honour in protecting the perpetrators of sexual harassment."

Mr Gleeson declined to comment in relation to Ms Foley's criticisms but expressed thanks for being informed of them.

On Monday last week, the High Court, under Chief Justice Susan Kiefel, revealed that an independent investigation it commissioned last year found Mr Heydon, when serving as a High Court judge, sexually harassed six female associates, including Ms Patterson Collins in 2005.

On the same day last week, Mr Heydon's lawyers issued a statement saying "our client denies emphatically any allegation of sexual harassment and any offence" and "any allegation of predatory behaviour or breaches of the law is categorically denied".

"Our client says that if any conduct of his has caused offence, that result was inadvertent and unintended, and he apologises for any offence caused."

Ms Foley is highly critical of Mr Gleeson's initial response of "I have nothing at all to say" when he was first asked to respond to the High Court investigation.

She is also highly critical that Mr Gleeson, when asked subsequently last week whether he had been informed by another judge, Michael McHugh, of the allegations against Mr Heydon he responded: "I do not discuss my conversations with Michael McHugh."

Ms Foley says of this response: "Again the culture of secrecy rears its head.

"It would be improper, so the thinking goes, for one judge to reveal his or her private conversations with another judge about court affairs.

"But surely the line must be drawn when these unwritten rules serve to protect a perpetrator of sexual harassment?

"Surely the unwritten rules must be put aside when the silence prevents a full inquiry into what was done at the time to protect Rachel Patterson Collins and those who came after her?"

She says Mr Gleeson's response "stands in contrast" to that of former chief justice Robert French, who succeeded Mr Gleeson in 2008. Mr Heydon was on the High Court from 2003 until 2013.

Mr French said he did not know of the allegations against Mr Heydon but made it clear he supported the action taken by Chief Justice Kiefel.

Ms Foley says Justice Kiefel, by commissioning the inquiry, had taken "an incredible step in the right direction".

The High Court inquiry, conducted by Vivienne Thom, had previously heard from an associate claiming at least two other judges at the time - Mr McHugh and Mr Gleeson - were told Mr Heydon had attempted to kiss one of his associates, Ms Patterson Collins.

Mr McHugh was allegedly made aware by his then associate Sharona Coutts. Mr McHugh said he informed Mr Gleeson.

Mr McHugh and Mr Gleeson declined to respond to requests for comment on this report.

HEADLINE: Suburb lockdowns loom for Victoria
TEXT:
Victoria will decide on suburb lockdowns within days as the state confirmed 75 new COVID-19 cases yesterday, pushing contact tracing to the limit and prompting experts to urge tougher measures to allow the rest of Australia's economy to reopen.

It is the first time since March that more than 70 new cases have been recorded in the state in a single day, and Victoria's Chief Medical Officer warned the outbreak "will get worse before it gets better".

Prime Minister Scott Morrison pledged to "do what is necessary to contain this outbreak".

He intended to canvass the possibility of hotspot lockdowns with Victorian Premier Daniel Andrews, but said that the state government would have the final say in what steps were taken.

"Victoria will lead that approach and they will be the final arbiter of what steps they take, but we can leave no stone unturned and no resource left unapplied to this task," Mr Morrison said. "I certainly will be considering all options and supporting the Premier in any such strong options that are necessary."

The federal and state governments were already providing "significant support" to Victoria with testing or contact tracing resources, as well as defence force involvement.

"We have seven states and territories at the moment in Australia where there is either no or virtually no community transmission," he said. "What that means is resources that are available in other states can also be deployed to assist ... Victoria."

Dr Sutton said the 75 new cases were "clearly big numbers" and "absolutely concerning", but that "we are not there yet" in terms of suburb lockdowns.

A suburb lockdown, which would involve ordering residents of particular postcodes or local governments to stay at home, would be difficult to police.

"We know it is a real challenge for businesses, it is a real challenge for people in their homes if that is what is required," he said. "We don't want to drive people out of suburban areas into new unaffected areas. So there is a balancing act in terms of making the call on a lockdown. But it is absolutely an option and we ... will use it if it is required."

Professor of epidemiology at Melbourne University Tony Blakely said it might be necessary to lock down more areas than just the hotspot suburbs to contain the virus.

"We are looking down the barrel of having to lock down all of Melbourne to contain infection to a level where Victoria can be part of the [national reopening] strategy," he said.

The spread of infection into other clusters and to railway stations, schools and hospitals meant it might be necessary to lock down more than just the hotspot suburbs, Professor Blakely said. If the rest of Australia was undertaking what essentially was an elimination, or near elimination strategy, then Victoria would need to do the same if the strategy of reopening borders and a return to normal living without restrictions was to work.

But this would require four weeks of lockdown and a return to the tight controls of March and April.

The AFL was forced to rejig its round-five schedule yesterday after Queensland introduced rules requiring all sporting teams to self-isolate for 14 days if they play a Melbourne team, play a match in Victoria, or face a team that has been in Victoria during the previous two weeks.

Richmond will now take on Melbourne in Victoria after originally being slated to battle West Coast on the Gold Coast this weekend.

The Gold Coast Suns will still head south to play Geelong in Victoria on Saturday, but then either go into quarantine or fly to another state after playing Hawthorn at the MCG in round six.

The A-League also relocated matches to a NSW hub in light of the Melbourne outbreaks.

The Western Australia government also shelved its plans to drop its border closure on August 8.

Spy boost to fight cyber wars
TEXT:
Canberra/Shanghai | An extra 500 cyber spies will be recruited as part of a $1.35 billion boost to protect the nation's sensitive computer networks and data from an unrelenting wave of cyber attacks which China is suspected of orchestrating.

Prime Minister Scott Morrison will unveil the 10-year funding commitment to enhance cyber security ahead of the release of a crucial Defence Department review that is expected to reaffirm the need to spend hundreds of billions of dollars on re-arming the military, including acquiring 12 submarines, because of a deteriorating regional strategic environment.

With relations between Canberra and Beijing already at a nadir, Chinese state-run newspaper The Global Times published a provocative story yesterday accusing Australia of intensifying an espionage campaign against China.

The accusations have been dismissed by China experts as a joke but in keeping with long-standing practice, the Morrison government is not commenting on intelligence matters.

"I wouldn't be relying on Chinese state media for your sources for questions," Mr Morrison said when asked about the story.

China's Foreign Ministry last night endorsed The Global Times piece as just the "tip of the iceberg" over allegations of Western intelligence gathering.

Following Mr Morrison's revelation 10 days ago a state-sponsored actor was behind a barrage of hacks targeting governments, businesses, critical infrastructure, health research and other organisations, the Prime Minister will go on a cyber war footing today.

The Cyber Enhanced Situational Awareness and Response, or CESAR, would identify more cyber threats, disrupt more foreign cybercriminals and build more partnerships between industry and government.

Headlining the package is $470 million to create more than 500 new jobs within the Australian Signals Directorate, the highly regarded agency responsible for thwarting cyber attacks. The ASD has a workforce of 1800 now.

ASD will also get a further $278 million to tackle offshore cybercrime; expand its data science and intelligence capabilities to stay ahead of emerging cyber threats; block and disrupt cyber attacks including sharing information with businesses in near real time; and developing a national situational awareness system to respond to threats on a national scale and assist vulnerable industries.

"The federal government's top priority is protecting our nation's economy, national security and sovereignty. Malicious cyber activity undermines that," Mr Morrison said.

"My government's record investment in our nation's cyber security will help ensure we have the tools and capabilities we need to fight back and keep Australians safe."

The cyber strategy is the entree to the release of the government's response tomorrow to a review of the Defence Force's structure, commissioned last year because of alarm over the acceleration in China's aggressiveness and American unpredictability under President Donald Trump.

The Australian Financial Review understands the 2020 Defence Force Structure plan will re-endorse the major projects the government plans to acquire, including building locally 12 submarines, nine frigates and hundreds of armoured vehicles, to maintain an effective deterrence and project force in the region.

The review is also expected to lock in extra funding for the military's command, communications and intelligence gathering systems. One source described this as "knitting" together the various systems so platforms such as ships and aircraft operate more seamlessly together, improving their potency in combat.

In addition to the traditional emphasis on air, land and sea and increasingly cyber, the review is also expected to counter emerging threats in space.

As Mr Morrison seeks to strengthen Australia's defences, the fiercely nationalistic Global Times claimed a compass and a map of Shanghai seized from alleged Australian spies arrested two years ago was evidence Australia was intensifying its spying of China.

In a series of bizarre claims citing a single anonymous source, the report claimed Australia was training agents at a Defence base in Victoria before sending them to China to spy, gather intelligence and recruit students and other citizens for espionage operations.

The allegations, which have not been reported in more credible state media outlets or confirmed by the Chinese government, were seen as a direct response to Mr Morrison's recent comments about the cyber attacks.

The report also followed ASIO's and the Federal Police raid on Friday on the home and parliamentary office of NSW Labor MP Shaoquett Moselmane over claims his office had been infiltrated by Chinese agents.

There are no public cases of Australian citizens being arrested in China in 2018 for espionage. Yang Hengjun, an Australian writer, has been detained in China since January 2019 on espionage allegations. Shang Baojun, a lawyer for Mr Yang, said yesterday he did not believe The Global Times' report was referring to that case.

The report carried photographs of what it called "espionage equipment" seized at the time which included cash, a USB flash drive, a notebook, a compass and a map of Shanghai.

The report also said Australian security agencies had set up an intelligence station in the Australian embassy in Beijing, where intelligence officers which had the status of diplomats were involved with inciting defections, intelligence gathering and cross-linking.

The report said Feng Chongyi, a Chinese-born academic living in Sydney who was detained during a visit to China in 2017, was an informant to Australian security intelligence agencies.

Professor Feng said the allegations were "outrageous slander".

"They know we won't take them to court so they can say anything," he told The Australian Financial Review.

A spokesman for China's Foreign Ministry said it was a "well-known fact" the Five Eyes intelligence network of Australia, the US, the UK, Canada and New Zealand had conducted large-scale internet monitoring and wiretapping against international law.

"As an important member of the Five Eyes Alliance, Australia has always played an active role in these activities," the spokesman said.

"For quite awhile, some Australians and media are enthusiastically fabricating all kinds of sensational Chinese espionage cases but they can never put up solid examples to prove their China infiltration theory.

"On the contrary, there are so many solid facts about the espionage activities conducted by Australia."

Australia-China Relations Institute head James Laurenceson said The Global Times piece was "bizarre".

"I'm getting to the point where I think some of these Global Times stories are so preposterous we have to remember what it's main objective is in the end and that is to generate clickbait," he said.

HEADLINE: Former Westpac boss in bid for MLC Wealth
TEXT:
Exclusive | One of the godfathers of the banking industry, David Morgan, pictured, is behind a bid to buy National Australia Bank's big superannuation and advice arm MLC Wealth. Street Talk can reveal one of Morgan's employers, American private equity firm JC Flowers, handed NAB an indicative bid for the business last week. Mr Morgan, a former Westpac chief, is heavily involved in the bid.
